lead: This unit teaches how to plan and design software tests, from a single test case to system acceptance. You will learn white-box and black-box methods, unit and integration testing, debugging and regression. After it, you can choose a test technique for a given requirement, compute basis paths, design boundary tests and explain where each testing level fits.
about: This unit turns testing from 'run it and see' into a planned set of comparisons. Chapter 4.1 fixes the vocabulary of defects and test cases. 4.2 separates verification from validation and QA from QC. 4.3 and 4.4 give the two main design methods: white-box tests from code structure and black-box tests from the specification. 4.5 applies test design at unit and integration level. 4.6 moves to system and acceptance testing and to debugging. 4.7 keeps old behaviour safe after a change. 4.8 covers non-functional tests: performance, stress, configuration and usability. 4.9 applies all of this to object-oriented, web and mobile systems.

chapters.idea: Testing is a controlled comparison of expected and actual behaviour; it can reveal defects but cannot prove their absence.
chapters.depth: Define error, fault, defect and failure with the chain error → fault → failure. A test case has an ID, purpose, preconditions, input data, steps, expected result and actual result; a test suite is a set of test cases. The test oracle is the source of the expected result. Cover the standard principles: testing shows presence of defects, exhaustive testing is impossible, early testing saves cost, defects cluster, the pesticide paradox, testing is context dependent, and the absence-of-errors fallacy. Some syllabi call a defect a bug and a test case a test specification. Ad-hoc testing is unscripted; keep it as a contrast, not a main method. Keep test-case writing as a template, not a full test plan.

figure.title: From test case to defect report

chapters.example: A bank ATM allows withdrawal from a savings account. Balance is ₹5,000. Test case TC1: withdraw ₹2,000 from an ATM with enough cash. Expected: dispense ₹2,000, balance ₹3,000, print receipt. TC2: withdraw ₹6,000. Expected: message 'Insufficient balance', no cash, balance stays ₹5,000. State which test passes if the ATM dispenses ₹2,000 but shows balance ₹3,500.
chapters.trap: Writing a test case with no expected result, or treating a failure as proof that every part of the program is wrong. A failure points to a fault; one fault can cause many failures.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 requirements, because a test case must trace to a requirement.
chapters.leave: Test plans, test teams, metrics and automation tools belong to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Verification checks the product against its specification; validation checks it against the user's real need; QA prevents defects in the process while QC detects defects in the product.
chapters.depth: Define verification ('are we building the product right?') and validation ('are we building the right product?'). Static verification uses desk checks, walkthroughs, reviews and inspections; dynamic validation uses testing. Some syllabi call desk checks deskchecks. Distinguish QA (process-oriented, preventive) from QC (product-oriented, detective). Include the V-model idea: each development phase has a matching test level. Coding standards are checked in code review. Keep review meeting roles and inspection checklists brief; Unit 6 covers technical reviews in detail.

figure.title: Verification and validation against a specification

chapters.example: A UPI app must let a user pay a ₹250 chai bill in under 30 seconds. Verification checks that the SRS says OTP is 6 digits and the design uses a 6-box OTP screen. Validation puts 10 users in front of the app and measures whether each can pay ₹250 in under 30 seconds. QA checks that every code change had a review before release; QC runs 40 payment tests on the release build. Which activity is which?
chapters.trap: Saying testing is only validation; reviews also test documents. Saying QA and QC are synonyms. Verification can be done without running code; validation cannot.
chapters.leave: Review meeting procedure, SQA organisation and metrics to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: White-box testing designs tests from the code's control flow; basis path testing gives a small set of independent paths that must be exercised.
chapters.depth: Also called structural, glass-box or clear-box testing. Cover statement, branch or decision, condition and path coverage. Draw a control flow graph (CFG): nodes are statements or blocks, edges are transfers of control. Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2P, where E = edges, N = nodes, P = connected components (usually 1). V(G) is the number of independent paths in a basis set, not all paths. List basis paths and choose inputs. Control structure testing adds condition testing, data flow testing and loop testing; only a few universities also teach symbolic execution and model checking here.
chapters.example: Consider the code: read n; if n > 0 then s = n + 1 else s = -n; if s > 10 then print 'large' else print 'small'. Draw its control flow graph, compute V(G), list three basis paths and give one input for each. V(G) = 9 edges - 8 nodes + 2 = 3. For n = 12, s = 13 and output is large: path 1-2-3-6-7-10. For n = -5, s = 5 and output is small: path 1-2-5-6-9-10. For n = 5, s = 6 and output is small: path 1-2-3-6-9-10.
chapters.trap: Counting all paths as V(G), or forgetting the +2P term. V(G) gives a basis, not every combination. Branch coverage at 100% does not guarantee condition coverage for compound decisions.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 test cases; basic programming control structures.
chapters.leave: Data flow testing and model checking details to advanced reading; test automation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Black-box testing designs tests only from the specification; equivalence partitioning groups inputs that should behave alike, and boundary value analysis tests the edges of those groups.
chapters.depth: Also called functional, specification-based or behavioural testing. Identify input and output domains. Split each domain into valid and invalid equivalence classes: one test per class. For a range a to b, boundary values are a−1, a, a+1, b−1, b, b+1; some syllabi call the extra outer values robustness testing. Cover equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and a simple decision table for combined rules. Mention pairwise or combinatorial testing only as a name; leave it to automation tools.
chapters.example: A railway booking form accepts passenger age as an integer from 1 to 120. A passenger aged 60 or more gets a senior discount. (a) List equivalence classes. (b) List boundary values for the range 1 to 120. (c) Give test cases for age 0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61, 119, 120 and 121 with expected accept or discount. Classes: below 1 invalid; 1 to 59 valid without discount; 60 to 120 valid with discount; above 120 invalid. Ages 0 and 121 are rejected; 1, 2 and 59 are accepted without discount; 60, 61, 119 and 120 are accepted with discount.
chapters.trap: Testing only the middle of a valid range and missing invalid classes. Treating 60 as an ordinary boundary when the requirement also has a senior-age boundary.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1; Unit 2 SRS for input rules.
chapters.leave: Combinatorial, pairwise and model-based black-box testing to tools and advanced reading.

chapters.idea: Unit testing checks one module in isolation using a driver and stubs; integration testing checks whether modules work together, using a chosen order and interface tests.
chapters.depth: Cover unit test planning, designing unit tests from detailed design, the test harness: a driver calls the unit under test, stubs replace modules the unit calls. Run tests, record pass or fail and defects. Integration strategies: big-bang, top-down (needs stubs), bottom-up (needs drivers), sandwich or hybrid, and incremental builds. Some syllabi call the test harness a unit test harness. Interface defects include wrong parameter order, missing data, incompatible types and timing. Keep system and acceptance testing for the next chapter.

figure.title: Unit under test with a driver and stubs

chapters.example: Unit calculateGST(amount, rate) returns amount × rate ÷ 100. Unit test: amount = ₹1,000, rate = 18, expected ₹180. The test driver calls the unit; a stub tax table returns 18 for 'GST'. Integration test: Billing calls calculateGST and Invoice. In top-down order, Billing is tested first with a stub Invoice that returns a fixed ₹1,180. Give one driver, one stub, and say what is tested in unit versus integration.
chapters.trap: Using a real database or network in a unit test. Swapping driver and stub: a driver calls the unit; a stub is called by the unit.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3 and 4 for test design; Unit 3 coupling for interfaces.
chapters.leave: System and acceptance testing to chapter 6; CI pipelines and test automation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: System testing checks the complete product against requirements; acceptance testing checks whether the customer will use it; debugging finds and repairs the cause of a failure.
chapters.depth: System testing: end-to-end functional tests plus recovery, security and other system qualities, but leave performance, stress and configuration to chapter 8. Scenario testing uses end-to-end user stories; keep it as system test design. Documentation testing checks user guides and help text against the product. Acceptance testing: user acceptance (UAT), alpha test at the developer's site, beta test at the user's site, contract and regulation acceptance. Some syllabi call these alpha-beta tests. Debugging is not testing: reproduce, diagnose, repair, then run regression tests. Debugging approaches: brute force, backtracking, cause elimination. A defect bash is a team bug-fix session; treat it as debugging, not a test level. Program analysis, symbolic execution and model checking are advanced; only a few universities teach them, so name the idea and skip proofs.

figure.title: System test, acceptance and debugging loop

chapters.example: A UPI app must transfer money between two accounts. System test: transfer ₹500 from account A (balance ₹2,000) to B (balance ₹1,000); expected A = ₹1,500 and B = ₹1,500. Acceptance test: 20 users each make 3 transfers; at least 18 of 20 must complete all 3 without help. During acceptance, one transfer shows B = ₹1,000 after the app says success. Write the debugging steps and the regression test to run after the fix.
chapters.trap: Calling debugging 'testing again'. Testing finds a failure; debugging finds the fault. Fixing the screen message without fixing the balance update is not debugging.
chapters.leave: Regression test selection to chapter 7; performance and stress to chapter 8; test reporting to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Regression testing reruns a chosen subset of existing tests after a change to show that unchanged behaviour still works.
chapters.depth: Define regression testing and regression test suite. Selection methods: retest-all, random selection, safe selection, and impact analysis or code-dependency selection. Prioritise tests by risk and frequent use. Maintain tests when expected outputs change. Smoke testing is a quick build check, not full regression. Some syllabi call it regression test selection. Keep CI automation for Unit 5; here focus on what to rerun and why.
chapters.example: An online store changes the GST rate on invoices from 18% to 12%. The full suite has 500 tests, the regression suite has 80 tests, and impact analysis selects 12 tests that touch invoice calculation. One old test for a ₹1,000 invoice expects tax ₹180. After the change the expected tax is ₹120. State what to rerun, which test must be updated, and why retest-all is not always the best choice.
chapters.trap: Rerunning the same old expected value after a deliberate requirement change, so a correct program looks wrong. Also, calling every retest a regression test without a selection reason.
chapters.leave: Automated regression in CI and version control to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Non-functional testing measures qualities: performance under load, behaviour beyond capacity, fitness across configurations, and ease of use including accessibility.
chapters.depth: Performance testing: response time, throughput (completed requests per second) and resource use under expected load; load testing runs at expected peak. Stress testing pushes beyond capacity and checks recovery. Configuration testing runs a matrix of hardware, OS, browser and network combinations; compatibility testing checks versions and devices. Usability testing observes real users completing tasks; accessibility testing checks keyboard, screen reader, contrast and text size. Some syllabi add internationalization testing (language, currency, date formats); mention it under configuration. Keep security testing out unless a syllabus adds it.
chapters.example: A ticket booking site is tested with 10,000 virtual users for 10 minutes. The target is 95% of searches under 3 seconds. Measured response times: at 5,000 users 1.4 s, at 10,000 users 2.8 s, at 20,000 users 5.6 s. Throughput at peak is 10,000 searches in 50 s. Compute throughput in searches per second. State one performance, one stress, one configuration and one usability test with numbers. Throughput = 10,000 ÷ 50 = 200 searches per second. Performance: 10,000 users, 2.8 s is within the 3 s target. Stress: 20,000 users, 5.6 s, then check recovery. Configuration: Chrome and Firefox on desktop and two Android versions. Usability: 8 of 10 users complete a booking in 2 minutes.
chapters.trap: Treating stress testing as the same as performance testing: stress looks beyond the limit and at recovery. Testing usability on one developer phone is not configuration testing.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6; Unit 3 UI design for usability.
chapters.leave: Security testing and penetration testing are separate; load-test tool scripting to Unit 5 automation.

chapters.idea: Object-oriented, web and mobile systems need tests that follow class inheritance and state, browser and server sessions, and device and network conditions.
chapters.depth: OO testing levels: method, class, cluster and system. Inheritance means a subclass must pass inherited tests plus its own; polymorphism means one call can run different methods, so test each actual type. State-based testing for objects with memory. Web testing: content, links, forms, cookies and session, navigation, browser compatibility, security basics and performance. Mobile testing: device and OS matrix, network changes, interruptions such as call, battery and low memory, location, installation and update, usability. Some syllabi call this testing OO systems and website testing. Keep functional test design from chapters 3 and 4; use chapter 8 for performance and configuration.
chapters.example: A payment system has base class Payment with method pay(amount). UPI and Card extend Payment and override pay(). A test creates Payment[] p = {new UPI(), new Card()}; p[0].pay(₹500) must use UPI and p[1].pay(₹500) must use Card. A web login form is tested on Chrome and Firefox; a mobile app is tested on 4 devices with network lost during a ₹500 payment. Write one OO test, one web test and one mobile test.
chapters.trap: Testing only the base class and not each subclass. On mobile, testing only one device and one network condition. On web, checking only the page loads and not the session or form rules.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3, 4 and 8; Unit 3 UML class diagrams and inheritance.
chapters.leave: Security testing, app-store release and device farm setup to Unit 5 and Unit 6.
